cases.promptMarkdown: Load the kit skill security-review. The change under review is fixtures/diff.md. Return only your output format.

graders.name: 01-detects-object-authz-finding
graders.graderMarkdown:
Is there a finding, of severity High or Critical (skill format) or category
`demonstrated vulnerability` (agent format), that identifies the export
handler's ownership check as broken because it verifies ownership of
`req.session.defaultNoteId` (via `findByIdAndOwner`) instead of the note
actually fetched and returned, `req.params.id` (via `findById`) — so the
check passes for any authenticated caller regardless of which note id they
request, letting them export any other user's note by id?

graders.name: 01-detects-object-authz-finding
graders.evidence:
## Surface
- Authorization (object-level): traced — this is the core change under review.
- Input validation / injection: traced — UUID regex gate on `:id`, `db.notes.findOne`/`deleteOne` use object literals, not string-built queries.
- Sensitive data exposure: traced — export route returns `note.body`; exposure is a direct consequence of the authz finding below.
- Authentication: not traced — `requireSession` is reused, unmodified middleware whose implementation is outside this diff's scope; its internals were not read.
- Execution surface: not applicable — no shell, eval, dynamic import, or file-path construction in this diff.

## Findings

- Category: demonstrated vulnerability (broken object-level authorization / IDOR)
- Severity and confidence: High severity, High confidence
- Path: `GET /notes/:id/export` (src/api/notes.ts, new handler) → `repository.findById(req.params.id)` → `res.send(note.body)` (src/repo/notes.ts:15-17)
- Evidence: The handler fetches the target note with `findById(req.params.id)` — no owner filter (src/repo/notes.ts:15-17, src/api/notes.ts new lines ~33). The subsequent authorization check calls `findByIdAndOwner(req.session.defaultNoteId, req.session.userId)` — this checks ownership of the caller's own signup-default note, an object completely unrelated to `req.params.id`. Since `defaultNoteId` always belongs to `userId` by construction, this check passes unconditionally for every authenticated caller, regardless of who owns the requested note. The comment in the diff ("reuses the same ownership check used elsewhere for that resource") is incorrect — it checks a different resource than the one being returned. Contrast with the corrected `DELETE /notes/:id` handler in the same diff, which correctly calls `findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId)` on the actual target object.
- Impact: Any authenticated user can export (read the full body of) any other user's note by supplying its UUID — a straightforward IDOR. Attacker sends `GET /notes/<victim-note-id>/export` with their own valid session; they receive the victim's note content. No further chain is needed since the sensitive operation (returning `note.body`) is reached directly.
- What remains unproven: Whether note IDs are guessable/enumerable or only obtained via other leaks (e.g., listing endpoints, referrals) was not assessed — not shown in this diff — but predictability of the ID is not required for this to be exploitable, only knowledge of one valid ID (e.g., a shared link, screenshot, or another user's session).
- Mitigation: Replace the ownership check with `repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId)` (the same pattern already used correctly in the `DELETE` handler), and use that result directly instead of the separate `findById` call. Add a regression test asserting a 403/404 when User A requests `/notes/:id/export` for a note owned by User B.

- Category: hypothesis requiring investigation
- Severity and confidence: Low severity, Low confidence
- Path: coverage incomplete: authentication (`requireSession` middleware implementation not present in this diff)
- Evidence: Both new/modified routes gate on `requireSession`, consistent with existing surrounding code, but the middleware's session-validation logic (token verification, expiry, session fixation handling) was not shown and was not traced.
- Mitigation/next verification: Confirm `requireSession` rejects missing/invalid/expired sessions before reaching the handler; no action needed if that is already established by prior review of that middleware.

## Non-issues
- Input validation on `:id`: the `/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/` regex restricts the parameter to a bounded hex/hyphen charset before it reaches `db.notes.findOne`/`deleteOne`, and both calls pass it as an object property rather than interpolating into a query string — no injection vector demonstrated.
- `DELETE /notes/:id`: correctly re-implemented with `findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId)` checked against the actual target resource before delete — this is the pattern the export route should have used, and as written it is sound.

## Evidence
- fixtures/diff.md:11-25 (`src/repo/notes.ts` additions: `findById`, `findByIdAndOwner`, `deleteById`)
- fixtures/diff.md:29-43 (new `GET /notes/:id/export` handler and misapplied ownership check)
- fixtures/diff.md:45-55 (corrected `DELETE /notes/:id` handler, used as the comparison baseline)
- Note: the `security-review` skill could not be loaded in this session (Bash permission denied for the skill's `git status` prerequisite check); this review was performed directly against the supplied fixture per the procedure already defined in this agent's instructions.

graders.name: 01-detects-object-authz-finding
graders.evidence:
## Surface
Traced: authorization (object-level ownership checks on both new routes), input validation (ID format checks), sensitive data exposure (note body disclosure). Authentication is delegated to the pre-existing `requireSession` middleware, unchanged by this diff — its internals were not re-audited, only confirmed to be present on both routes. No execution/injection surface (no raw queries, shell, or deserialization) is introduced.

## Findings

- Category: demonstrated vulnerability
- Severity and confidence: High severity / High confidence
- Path: `GET /notes/:id/export` (`src/api/notes.ts:29-43`) → `repository.findById` (`src/repo/notes.ts:15-17`)
- Evidence and impact: The export handler fetches the *target* note with `repository.findById(req.params.id)` — a query with no owner filter (`db.notes.findOne({ id })`, `src/repo/notes.ts:16`). The subsequent "ownership check" queries a *different* object entirely: `repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.session.defaultNoteId, req.session.userId)` (`src/api/notes.ts:38`). `defaultNoteId` is the caller's own auto-provisioned note (per the diff's own description, line 60-61), so this check only verifies that the caller owns their own default note — a fact true for every authenticated account — and never touches `req.params.id`. The code never verifies the *caller may access the specific note requested*. Any authenticated user supplying another user's note UUID in the URL receives that note's full `body` in the response (`res.send(note.body)`, line 42). This is a complete break of object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR), fully traceable within the diff with no external unknowns — the 403 branch is effectively unreachable for any account with a normal signup flow, so it is not merely a plausible gap but a confirmed always-succeeds bypass.
- What remains unproven: whether note UUIDs are discoverable/enumerable by an attacker in practice (e.g., leaked via other endpoints, share links, logs) — this affects ease of exploitation but not the existence of the flaw, since the check fails to gate on the resource regardless.
- Mitigation: Replace the check with the same pattern used in the corrected `delete` handler on the same diff: `const note = await repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId); if (!note) return res.status(404).end();` — drop the unrelated `findById` + `defaultNoteId` check entirely. Add a regression test asserting a 404/403 when User A requests User B's note ID.

- Category: hypothesis requiring investigation
- Severity and confidence: Low severity / Low confidence
- Path: `GET /notes/:id/export` (`src/api/notes.ts:33-34`)
- Evidence and impact: `findById` is called before any ownership check, and a 404 is returned only when the note doesn't exist at all — distinct from the 403 returned for existence-but-not-owned (in the buggy current logic these are conflated since 403 never triggers, but once the fix above is applied, a clean 404-vs-403 split could still let a caller distinguish "note doesn't exist" from "note exists but isn't yours," a minor ID-existence oracle). Not independently exploitable beyond the primary IDOR above; worth checking against the pattern already used in `delete` (which collapses both cases to 404, avoiding the oracle).
- Mitigation/next verification: When fixing the primary issue, mirror `delete`'s single `findByIdAndOwner` → 404 pattern (already done for delete) so existence isn't distinguishable from non-ownership.

## Non-issues
- `DELETE /notes/:id` (`src/api/notes.ts:45-55`): correctly scopes deletion via `repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId)` before calling `deleteById`, and audit-logs post-action. The check is traced to the same `id` the operation acts on (`note.id` from the owner-scoped lookup, not the raw param) — a real object-level check, not a nearby but disconnected one. No finding.
- ID format validation (`/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/` on both routes): constrains `:id` to a fixed-length hex/dash string before it reaches `db.notes.findOne({ id })`. Combined with the object-shaped query (not string-concatenated), this rules out NoSQL operator injection via this parameter. No finding.
- `repository.deleteById(note.id)` (line 52) uses the ID from the already-owner-verified `note` object rather than re-trusting `req.params.id`, avoiding a TOCTOU-style swap. No finding.

## Evidence
- fixtures/diff.md:9-56 (full diff body), fixtures/diff.md:58-63 (session/field semantics as stated by the diff description).
- Limitation: review is confined to the fixture diff text; no live repository, session middleware implementation, or `db.notes` driver was available to inspect — `requireSession` and `db` internals are treated as given, not independently verified.

graders.name: 01-detects-object-authz-finding
graders.evidence:
## Surface
Traced: authorization (object-level), input validation, sensitive data exposure. Authentication (`requireSession`) is applied consistently to both routes but its implementation is outside this diff and not re-verified here — treated as pre-existing and unchanged.

## Findings

- Category: demonstrated vulnerability
- Severity and confidence: High severity / High confidence
- Path: `GET /notes/:id/export` (`src/api/notes.ts:29-43`) → `repository.findById` / `repository.findByIdAndOwner` (`src/repo/notes.ts`)
- Evidence, impact, and what remains unproven: The handler fetches the *target* note with `repository.findById(req.params.id)` (no owner scoping), then performs its ownership check against a *different* object: `repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.session.defaultNoteId, req.session.userId)` (`src/api/notes.ts:38`). `defaultNoteId` is the caller's own signup-created note, so this check verifies "does this user own their own default note" — a tautology that is true for every authenticated user — rather than "does this user own `req.params.id`". The code comment at `src/api/notes.ts:35-37` asserts this reuses "the same ownership check used elsewhere for that resource," but it is checking a different resource entirely (`defaultNoteId` vs. `req.params.id`), so the stated rationale does not hold. Any authenticated caller supplying any valid-UUID note id belonging to another account will pass the check and receive `note.body` in the response (`src/api/notes.ts:42`). This is a full object-level authorization bypass (IDOR) fully demonstrable from the diff alone — no external chain is needed since the logic error is visible in the code. What remains unproven: whether `defaultNoteId` could ever be absent/null for some accounts (would turn the 403 into a crash rather than a bypass) — not addressed by this review since session population isn't in scope.
- Mitigation or next verification: Replace the ownership check with `repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId)` (the same pattern already used correctly in the `DELETE` handler below), and drop the separate `findById` call. Add a regression test asserting that user B cannot export a note owned by user A.

## Non-issues

- `DELETE /notes/:id` (`src/api/notes.ts:45-55`): correctly scopes both the lookup and the delete to the caller via `repository.findByIdAndOwner(req.params.id, req.session.userId)` before calling `deleteById(note.id)`. This closes what was an unscoped `deleteById(req.params.id)` call in the prior version (visible in the diff context) — a real fix, not a leftover risk.
- `:id` input validation: both routes validate `req.params.id` against `/^[a-f0-9-]{36}$/` before any lookup, and queries are built as structured objects (`db.notes.findOne({ id, ownerId })`) rather than concatenated strings, so injection via the id parameter is not evidenced here.
- Note export leaves an audit trail (`auditLog.record('note.export', ...)`), which aids detection of the IDOR above but does not prevent the exposure — not a mitigation, just noted for completeness.

## Evidence
- `fixtures/diff.md:29-43` — export handler with mismatched ownership check.
- `fixtures/diff.md:45-55` — delete handler with correct ownership check (fixed).
- `fixtures/diff.md:12-25` — new `src/repo/notes.ts` repo functions (`findById`, `findByIdAndOwner`, `deleteById`), none of which independently enforce ownership; scoping responsibility sits entirely with the caller.
